title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden Picks 05: Ballern, Giawasa, Huettel, Manitou, Marenda, Rheintritt, Syre, Ten:07, Wizard Works – Paul Kalifatidi & John Watson
content:
Guten morgen! We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. Paul and John spent the weekend at the world’s largest framebuilder showcase, selecting bikes to document for The Radavist’s coverage of the event. Check out our picks 05 from Ballern, Giawasa, Huettel, Manitou, Mareda, Rheintritt, Syre, ten:07, and Wizard Works below!

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

Ballern Stainless All-Road – John Watson

Hamburg-based Ballern Cycleworks has a fondness for stainless steel and raw brass fillets. While catching up with builder and party boy Bennet Janz, he brought me up to speed on updates with his career. A metalworker by education and trade, Bennet spends his professional time mostly building out metalwork installs for bars, nightclubs, and the occasional residential project. Ballern Cycleworks is mostly a sig gig for him now, but that doesn’t mean he gives it any less care.

As evident by this stunning carbon and stainless all-road bike, which maxes out tire clearance on the fork in favor of tight clearances, aka the track bike aesthetic. “The tires say 32 mm but they ballooned out much bigger, almost 34 mm, so it’s tight in the fork!” he commented as I pored over the bike’s detailing.

Being for a tall customer, Bennet has yet to do the final fit check on the bike, which will lower the saddle and stem by a few millimeters. “Right now the post and steerer are uncut. I’m dialing the client’s fit in this week,” he noted. Ballern’s bikes always excude a beautiful balance between tech and tradition, with beautiful fillets left raw atop the stainless steel tubing.

This tall all-road had my heart doing all sorts of pitter-pattering. Plus, Bennet always brings the sexy!

@BallernCycleworks

Giawasa NJS Track Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

At every bike show, I feel like I have this silly award I keep in my head. It’s for the “nicest person” and it is always stiff competition amongst the unknowing competitors. It was no different at Bespoked Dresden, and frankly, I think it’s going to remain a tie between many for first place. One person that made a lasting impression on me was Jergen Gertze of Giawasa.

Jergen is a kindergarten teacher and the first bike he ever made was a lovable little strider for his students. It’s clearly been well loved and had perhaps the strongest patina of any bike at the show. It looks like every kids bike should look. For his second frame, Jergen made himself the perfect play thing, a stunning Cinelli Laser inspired track bike to which Paul Declercq of Slow Spin Society gave the “best track bike” award. I know that builders love their bikes, but I have never seen someone so clearly show it as Jergen. While doing my best to focus on the bike, I kept panning the camera up to Jergen as it was clear just how much this bike meant to him.

Track bikes are a frequent starting point for beginner framebuilders as they have the least demanding designs. There are no brake mounts to worry about, cable routing doesn’t have to be sorted, and tire clearance is simple. But, this means that it is far harder to hide any inconsistencies or asymetries. The kindergarten strider certainly has some funny angles, but I think that is what makes it so lovable. The track bike, on the other hand, is damn-near perfect. Even the “aero” bracing came out quite clean.

The fork features a lugged crown made by Tetsuro Harada, the master builder of Samson Bicycles in Japan. The bike is built up using Japanese NJS components, a niche of the industry that Jergen fell in love with when getting into bikes. The aero elements of the frame are inspired by the iconic Cinelli Laser. Meeting builders like Jergen and hearing how a bicycle came to be – what inspired it’s inception and the background of the builder – is the point of these shows, and I love finding the stories and doing my best to share them.

Jergen, thank you for being one of the kindest people I ever met. I also work with children and I know how much patience and care it takes. I’m excited to watch your framebuilding journey and can’t wait to see what you come up with next.

@Giawasa

Huettel Cycles 32er SSMTB – John Watson

Big bike. Check. Lavender. Check. Segmented fork. Check. Portage handle. Check. This Huettel Cycles 32er SSMTB caught my eye immediately during the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show. “Now that’s a Radavist reader…” I thought to myself as I passed by Jonas Huettel’s busy show booth. Every time I walked past, he was deep in conversation, and not wanting to interrupt a potential customer, I kept my distance.

On Sunday, the last day of the show, I finally caught up with Jonas, a new builder out of Markneukirchen, Germany. He was indeed a fan of The Radavist, and immediately told me that the paint was inspired by an early 1990s Ibis MTB. He built every primary part on the bike. Frame. Fork. Stem. And even the titanium seatpost.

His segmented fork was stunning. As were the tire alignments and clever, subtle details like the brake stiffener in the rear stays. The post was milled by hand in his shop, a process that takes an incredibly long time due to titanium’s hardness. Jonas’ approach to 32er geometry was to increase the frame’s scale by 10% and steepen the head tube angle to make the steering more nimble for the wagon wheels. His angles of preference were 69º head tube and 75º seat tube.

Which, as you can see, keeps the bike light underfoot. I’d yet to get a wheelie photo at the show, but he gladly rode a long, 100-meter wheelie in the middle of the Dresden airport, with a big smile on his face.

Well done, Jonas!

@HuettelCycles

ManitouFS I and Gamux FS II – John Watson

“Brand legacy is something you have to nurture. You’ve gotta feed it. Or the brand will die.” Josh Riddle commented as I faffed with my photo stick while shooting the Manitou FS II. Inspired by Doug Bradbury’s original Manitou full suspension, the US framebuilder made in 1993, the Manitou FS II is a modern, European take on the original concept. Manitou is a brand with a healthy legacy, and as my review of the Mattoc Pro earlier this year noted, the brand continues to make exceptional suspension products.

Taking the Manitou FS concept into the future, Manitou partnered with Gamux, a Swiss bike company, to deliver a collaborative effort alongside Pinion, Gates, Schwalbe, Hayes, ProTaper, and Reynolds. The FS II is a forward-thinking, modern twist on the original Manitou FS bike. Check out a deep dive on the FS II at Manitou.

It features a monocoque frame with a unique linkage design at the dropout and pinion gearbox yoke. Like the original, the FS II utilizes a Manitou fork on the front and rear seat stay. Manitou’s bikes are iconic and have pushed the envelope since its founding in 1986, and this retro-inspired FS II is no different.

Josh and I went to high school together in Wilmington, NC. At the time, cycling wasn’t really our thing, aside from a BMX bike and a cruiser I’d ride to the beach with my surfboard or skateboard, but here we are, over twenty-seven years later, at a bike show in Germany, catching up.

@Manitou @GamuxBikes

Marenda Cycles Full Suspension – Paul Kalifatidi

Denis Uzelac is the builder of this stupendous steel steed. He lives in Switzerland, and if you’re unfamiliar, they have hills and chocolate, among other things. Hills and chocolate are two of my favorite things, therefore, I must visit at some point. Denis raved about the mountain biking but he forgot to mention the chocolate.

I have some bad news: this bike is Denis’s personal bike and you’re unlikely to be able to buy one. The wild suspension design is simply too complex and time consuming to make at any sort of scale. And yet, Denis felt motivated to make one for himself, again exemplifying the level of experimentation and capability that were on display at Bespoked Dresden.

A previous draft of this suspension construction featured four smaller tubes for the shock tunnel rather than the two-tube version that you see in the photos. I would I would have loved to see the build process in-person. How cool would it be if Bespoked was a few months long and all the builders had to bring their workshop to the venue and make their bike there? Constantine Drust has a hilarious story about his old shipping container workshop almost falling off of a forklift.

Denis’s bike was finished just in time for the show and not in time for any type of paint job. That’s ok, because I have a feeling that he is going to modify the design and continue to tinker far before the paint would have time to dry. Denis, thanks for hanging out. You have an infectious laugh!

@MarendaCycles

Rheintritt High Pivot MTB – Paul Kalifatidi

Sitting at the Microshift Booth, at the top of the second set of escalators, showgoers were greeted by this stunning mountain bike from Rheintritt. I, too, like many, was captivated by its steel bike silhouette. The bike is made out of 3d printed lugs, carbon tubes, and a billet aluminum rear triangle. I met Phillip, who makes every Rheintritt, to get the lowdown on all of this bike’s quirks and features.

Ok, there aren’t many quirks, with the exception of Rheintritt’s hilarious head tube badge that features an ice cream cone. There are many features. I was instantly captivated by the myriad of geometry and travel permutations offered by the suspension design. The stroke, length, and shock mount position – both top and bottom – can all be changed for a damn-near infinite amount of tinkering. For some, that’s way too many options in which you could get lost. For others, this is exactly why they might want a custom bike like this Rheintritt.

The bike is also rated for a dual-crown fork, in case you want to spend a lot of time at the bike park. Fred, Phillip’s friend, had his personal pink version of the bike at the show with such a build. His bike was even equipped with a limited-edition brake set of the Die Bremse RS from 612 Components, a fellow German brand. These things are as hot as the bike they’re built to stop. They had a very interesting feel: there wasn’t a firm bite point but rather a very gradual build-up of pressure. I’m curious if they offer a high degree of braking granularity and would love to get my paws on some.

To entertain bike park laps, this frame had to be built crazy strong. For example, the downtube is 4mm thick, which is a lot for a carbon fiber tube. Phillip could have gone for a larger diameter tube, which might have weighed slightly less, but he wanted to maintain the thin tube profile. I love that look. When the mainstream bike industry seems set on making bicycles look like electric motorcycles, Phillip’s vision is refreshing.

Phillip doesn’t just make these wild gravity sleds; he had a variety of bike phenotypes on display at the show, including an adorable cargo mini-velo. His talent and desires have depth, a theme I saw repeated time and time again at Bespoked Dresden. Phillip, thank you for your vision. Please, more of it!

@RheintrittBikes

Syre Puncake Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Perhaps one of the more memorable parts of Bespoked Dresden was meeting fellow Russian speakers. For our European listeners, this might seem a bit silly as plenty of Russians have relocated to mainland Europe over the years and particularly over the last five. But, I don’t often get to speak Russian with anybody but my family, and certainly very few people in the American bike industry. Fortunately, I met the guys at Raketa and Bjorn Components. Both companies make all of their products in Europe. Raketa machines various crankset, chainring, and hub components while Bjorn makes stunning carbon fiber touch points like saddles, seatposts, and handlebars. They collaborated on the build for this made in Saint Petersburg Syre gravel bike. It’s a pretty sweet rig: 2.5 inch tire clearance with race pace chainring sizes.

Puncake is a portmanteau of punk and pancake; the makers of Syre identify as punks and everybody loves pancakes. Seems simple to me. It is made out of a monocoque front triangle and the rear frame parts are bonded in later. This differs slightly from the other carbon fiber bikes that I have photographed at this show which mostly featured an entirely lugged construction. The advantage of building a one piece triangle is a potentially lighter and stronger frame, and it comes with the downside of cost and complexity because of the required size run of molds. This is the first bike show where I paid close attention to the carbon fiber bikes and I’m realizing that the greater variety of construction methods opens up lots of interesting work for builders.

If using a two-headed horseman as a metaphor, the Syre Puncake is a wonderfully light and capable bike that leans more towards the Dangerholm-esque head of this mythical creature. The other head, of course, is Ronnie Romance.

Thank you to all of the guys at Bjorn and Raketa. I know I have a bizarre non-American-not-quite-Russian accent. Meeting you meant a lot, more than you could ever imagine.

@Syre @Bjorn @Raketa

ten:07 Unicorn Pony Trail Cago – Paul Kalifatidi

The name ten:07 has such a great origin story. When Daniel Ghirtoi was working at Enigma Bikes, he had a Casio watch with broken buttons. At one point, he had set an alarm for 10:07 and was now unable to change it or turn it off. Therefore, every day, his alarm went off. He decided to turn it into snack time, and the snack of choice was a banana. Fast forward to today, and Daniel owns his own cargo bike company, hence the pack-mule headtube badge. The donkey’s ears point to 10:07, and the banana leads into the world.

The Unicorn Pony is the brand’s smallest bike, hence the pony nomenclature. It can fit big tires, and I really like the way these aggressive-tread Schwalbe Big Betty tires contrast against the titanium frame. It was awarded the “best off-road” prize. Should you want to get extra rowdy, the front rack is removable for easier trail viewing. A variety of front platforms will be available.

This Unicorn Pony can be run with a chain- or belt-driven drivetrain. I guess it can also be built up single-speed, should carog masochism be your idea of a good time. The steel frame is currently available for pre-order on the ten:07 website, and the Taiwan-made titanium version will be available shortly.

Daniel, thank you for showing me your little horse. I really like it!

@Ten07

Wizard Works and Clandestine Touring Hardtail – Paul Kalifatidi

Dear Harry and Veronica, you are two people, and being two people, it is impossible for me to split my imaginary “nicest person award” in two. Sadly, that eliminated you from the competition. I hope you understand. Kindly, Paul. Ok, now about the bags and the bike. Yes, you see it correctly; those are purple and pink bags on a yellow Clandestine. Yes, I think it’s as cool as you think it is too.

Harry and Veronica, and their small team, make every Wizard Works product in their London workshop. Fittingly, they brought a made-in-Devon, UK, Clandestine hardtail to display their bags. Both of them have their own personal Clandestine bikes, but they figured a new one had to enjoy the spotlight. Pi Manson of Clandestine made this bike for their friend.

The bike is a trail-capable touring hardtail. Perhaps my favorite adjectives to describe a hardtail. A Matching but easily removable rear rack makes it easy to go from jump and jam mode to tent and too tired mode. Oh also, Harry and Veronica, I just noticed the tiny seat tube brace and WHY IS THERE NO TINY BAG IN THERE. I’m losing my mind, I know. Two big bike shows in a month, and the noisy voices start to come out.

I first saw a Wizard Works bag when I was working at Angry Catfish in Minneapolis. Then, like now, what stood out were the thoughtful color choices and range of fabric textures that work as well together as they do apart. I never thought that I would meet the whizzes that work on these bags six years later. I’m still pinching myself that I get to do this for a job.

@WizardWorks @Clandestine
